title.official: Reviewing lawyer’s charges: incomplete services and particular events

division.heading: Lawyers’ Charges, Retainer Agreements and Right of Review

operative_text.controlling:
10.24(1)  If any of the following events occurs, a lawyer, the
lawyer’s personal representative or a client may make an
appointment with a review officer for the purpose of determining
the amount of the lawyer’s charges payable by the client:
(a) the lawyer dies;
(b) the lawyer is suspended, disbarred or incapacitated;
(c) the lawyer ceases to be the client’s lawyer or the client
ceases to be the lawyer’s client;
(d) a dispute arises about the apportionment of contingency
fees under a contingency fee agreement under which 2 or
more lawyers are engaged, whether or not the contingency
has occurred;
(e) the client retains a new lawyer in the action;
(f) the client unreasonably discontinues or abandons any
matter to which a contingency fee agreement applies;
(g) any other event that creates uncertainty about a lawyer’s
charges or who is to pay them or to whom they are to be
paid.
(2)  When making a decision under this rule, the review officer
must take into consideration the factors described in rule 10.2,
except to the extent that a retainer agreement otherwise provides.

BOOK_B.title: Reviewing lawyer's charges: incomplete services and particular events

commentary.text: Rule 10.24 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.24. In Lising v. Smith, 2018 ABQB 1061, 2018 CarswellAlta 3189, Justice Shelley had before her an appeal by a lawyer from a Review Officer's decision in relation to a retainer agreement between the lawyer and his then client. The lawyer submitted that the “Review Officer ought not to have reviewed his [the lawyer's] account because more than six months had passed between the date [the lawyer] sent the account [to the client] and the date the Appointment for Review was filed.” Justice Shelley found that the lawyer “did not complete the services contemplated in the Retainer Agreement. He was suspended [by the Law Society], the result of which is that he ceased to be capable of completing the services because he could no longer be the Respondents' lawyer.” Justice Shelley found that Rule 10.24 applied, that Rule 10.24 was not subject to the time limitation set out in Rule 10.10(2). Her Ladyship said: [21]… More importantly, Rule 10.24 is a separate Rule specific to this circumstance and does not contain any limitation on a client's right to have a lawyer's charges reviewed where, for any of the reasons set out in that Rule, a lawyer is unable to complete the services for which the lawyer was retained. [22] I therefore reject Mr. Smith's argument that the Review Officer should not have reviewed the October 3, 2017 invoice on the basis that he was precluded from doing so by virtue of Rule 10.10(2).
